the optical detection limits of molecular interactions are limited by refractive index changes associated with the binding event and that the magnitude of the optical refractive index changes are a strong function of the size of the interacting species.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the detection limit of BSI is not yet known.
the BSI signal is not solely due to refractive index change, and that the BSI detection limit is not limited by refractive index change alone.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

optical sensing of protein interactions can be made sensitive to the nanomolar concentration of the analyte, but only if the optical refractive index contrast between the interacting species is large.

the detection limit of molecular interactions in free-solution is limited not just by the magnitude of the refractive index changes but by the magnitude of optical scattering from the interacting particles.
the detection limit for optical sensing of protein interactions is not limited by the optical refractive index changes but rather by the signal to noise ratio of the optical detection system.
The main takeaway from our work is that

for optical sensing techniques that rely on refractive index change for detection, the detection limit is determined by a combination of the refractive index sensitivity, the concentration of the interacting species, the association rate constant, and the equilibrium constant of the reaction.

the optical detection limit for molecular sensing can be estimated from a few easily measured quantities, and the model provides a general framework for designing experiments for optimizing the optical signal.

the detection limit in optical sensing is not only a function of the concentration and the size of the molecules, but also the nature of the interaction, the refractive index of the medium and the surface chemistry.
